When we speak, we not only present information for discussion, but we may also signal our degree of commitment to that information. Evidentials, linguistic expressions that we use to signal the kind of evidence that we have for our claims (visual or hearsay for example), are often argued to modulate the expressed degree of commitment (e.g., Faller, 2002). This study aims to gather reliable empirical data on the role of so-called reportative evidentials (like ‘I heard that Jack is a bachelor’) in impacting the degree of perceived speaker commitment (here, their commitment to the truth of Jack being a bachelor).

The hearsay expression altogether removes the speaker’s commitment, since the speech act merely commits the speaker to having heard someone say the propositional content, and not to the truth of that content. This is the position that Faller (2002) advocates for the reportative evidential ‘-si’ in Cuzco Quechua, for example, and Murray (2014) for ‘I heard that …’ in English.

The speaker remains consistently committed to the proposition, and the reportative evidential merely provides further information about the source of evidence. This is what Hunter (2016) for example claims for English parenthetical ‘…, she said’.

The reportative evidential reduces, but does not altogether remove, the speaker’s commitment to the truth of the proposition. Koev (2021) advocates this position for English embedding ‘She said that …’ and parenthetical ‘… , she said.’ This answer suggests that commitment is a matter of degree, rather than an all-or-nothing notion.

In (2), the clause expressing the propositional content that Jack is a bachelor is embedded with respect to the reportative main clause. By contrast, in (3) the propositional content forms the main clause, and due to its prominence, may perhaps be interpreted as the ‘main point’ of the utterance (Simons, 2007). The reportative evidential is here included as ‘just’ a parenthetical clause. As a consequence, several authors have expressed the intuition that parenthetical constructions lead to a greater speaker commitment to the expressed content than embedding ones.2

To answer these questions of commitment, we study the felicity of denying the expressed proposition. It is generally infelicitous as a speaker to deny propositions to which one has previously committed: ‘p, (but) not p’ or ‘I know that p, (but) not p’. One can take felicity of such denials as a starting point for a test of commitment, used in, for example, Bonalumi et al. (2023) and Weissman 2022), but we find the idea already in Asher (2000), Jackendoff (1972), and many others. In the case of the simple assertion in (1), it would be decidedly odd for the speaker to continue with ‘But he’s married.’ However, what if the speaker continues in the same way after an utterance of (2) or (3)? Here intuitions already become much less clear. This is a more general complication: judgments regarding speaker commitment are often very subtle and nuanced (Mazzarella et al., 2018).

For this reason, we choose to take an experimental approach to the felicity of denying the expressed proposition. Specifically, we use facial electromyography (fEMG), a physiological method measuring facial muscle activity. This technique enables researchers to precisely target specific muscles, which can be mapped onto participants’ emotional states, thereby providing information about the valence and intensity of their affective responses (Ekman et al., 1972; van Boxtel, 2010). There is a large literature showing that the corrugator supercilii muscle (the inner-eyebrow muscle used for frowning)—whose activation is associated with negatively valenced affective responses—becomes active in cases of norm violations (Bartholow et al., 2001; ’t Hart et al., 2018; van Berkum et al., 2023). In previous work, we have shown that this extends to the communicative norm that one should not contradict their own prior commitments (Yates et al., 2025). In that study, we showed that the corrugator becomes highly active when participants read about a speaker who denies an earlier asserted proposition, in contrast to when the same proposition was posed as a question. That is, an observer frowns when witnessing a commitment violation. This study suggests that fEMG offers a reliable way to measure the assignment of speaker commitment in communication.
fEMG allows precise, muscle-specific measurement, enabling researchers to trace the emotional response of indignation triggered by a commitment violation (Bartholow et al., 2001).

fEMG offers high sensitivity, detecting subtle facial muscle activity (including nonvisible contractions), capturing responses before or without overt expressions (Rutkowska et al., 2024; van Boxtel, 2010).

fEMG provides an implicit measure of immediate, spontaneous affective response (even preconscious and involuntary, Cacioppo et al., 2000), capturing reactions that could otherwise be lost when participants must reflect or articulate explicit judgments. This reduces the potential impact of self-modulation or social desirability bias, wherein participants may consciously or unconsciously adjust their true responses in order to align with perceived expectations or to present themselves in a favourable light (Crowne & Marlowe, 1960; Dodou & de Winter, 2014).

fEMG delivers high temporal resolution, with detectable activity known to emerge as early as 100–200 ms from stimulus onset, allowing affective responses to be tracked as they unfold, and enabling the use of fine-grained analyses such as time-course modeling to reveal nuanced dynamics (e.g., ’t Hart et al., 2018; van Boxtel, 2010).

fEMG, through baseline-normalized microvolt activity, offers an objective and standardized metric that accounts for individual differences (e.g., in physiological capacity, some people simply have stronger corrugator muscles than others). This normalization enables reliable inter- and intra-participant comparisons, ensuring that a participant with weaker absolute responses is not less valuable to the overall picture (van Boxtel, 2010; van Boxtel & van der Graaff, 2024).

One remark about the theoretical framework before we proceed. There are two main stances on what the primary effect of assertions is. In this paper we opt for a commitment-based framework in which a plain assertion of (1) has as its primary consequence that the speaker becomes committed to the truth of the propositional content (e.g., Hamblin, 1971). There is also an alternative take on assertions in which they primarily convey beliefs and intentions. The most explicit defenders of this second approach are Bach and Harnish (1979), who claim that by asserting that p the speaker expresses the belief that p and the intention that the hearer believe that p.

In the philosophy of language, where this is a central debate, the social and normative character of commitments gets much attention. We find this approach for example in Brandom (1983); Geurts (2019); Hamblin (1971); Krifka (2015); MacFarlane (2011); Searle (1976). Following this tradition we define a commitment in general as an obligation to others to act in certain ways. By our linguistic acts, we create expectations for our conversational partners, who in turn are entitled to expect us to act consistently with our prior commitments. Commitments thus constrain how we should behave. In the specific case of assertions, our commitments concern the truth of the contents that we express. While opinions differ on what exactly this entails (e.g., Brandom (1983) argues this is justificatory responsibility to the truth when challenged, whereas MacFarlane (2011) argues that this is too strong), at the very minimum it entails that one should not continue by asserting something that is inconsistent with an earlier assertion, and that is what we will make use of in this study.

In more empirical linguistic work the notion of commitment is used in the analysis of many linguistic phenomena (discourse particles, evidentiality markers, intonation) and the idea of a conversational scoreboard of commitments is, for example, central in Faller (2019), Farkas and Bruce (2010), Gunlogson (2008), Krifka (2015, 2023), Portner (2018), and much subsequent work. The difference between (private) beliefs and (public) commitments is often mentioned, but the normative dimension does not always get much attention. Still, in a light version this dimension is present here, too: a speaker should not contradict themselves.

Nothing in our present study hinges on one’s position within this debate. While it is in general important to distinguish beliefs and commitments (e.g., Bary, 2025; Geurts, 2019), they often go hand in hand, and what differs is just who is in the driver’s seat and who follows in the back seat (Geurts, 2019). Readers who favor a belief-and-intention view on assertion may thus want to reinterpret our question of commitment in terms of certainty (‘Is a speaker who includes a marker of hearsay evidence perceived as expressing greater uncertainty compared to the plain assertion?’) and the increased corrugator activity may then be a sign of the emotion of confusion rather than indignation (Durso et al., 2012). So, our study cannot be used to differentiate between the commitment-based and belief-and-intention-based accounts of communication.

This brings us to our hypotheses. The speech act of a plain assertion is seen as a relatively uncontroversial way to take on commitments in communication in the literature; someone who makes an assertion takes on a commitment to the truth of the proposition they express (Brandom, 1983; Geurts, 2019; Hamblin, 1971; Searle, 1976). This commitment entails that the speaker will be taken to be violating a norm if they continue by asserting something that is inconsistent with the earlier asserted proposition. Reportative evidentials, by contrast, are often claimed to reduce the speaker’s commitment. On the basis of this, we hypothesize that (i) plain assertion–incongruent should elicit higher corrugator activation than the ‘I heard’ conditions, since in this case the speaker has undertaken the clearest and strongest commitment to their initial asserted propositions, making the subsequent contradiction a greater violation. The reportative evidential constructions should elicit lower corrugator activation.

The sample size was determined primarily by practical constraints, including the financial resources available for participant compensation, the time required for recruitment and testing, and the availability of testing facilities. Individual testing sessions lasted approximately 90 mins, and recruitment took approximately three months to complete. Nevertheless, the resulting sample is large compared to similar previous studies (e.g., Bartholow et al., 2001; Durso et al., 2012; Thompson et al., 2016).

Finally, 32 filler item sets were included for two purposes. One was to reduce predictability and distract participants from the experimental manipulations. The second was to ensure that any observed corrugator activity could indeed be attributed to a commitment violation, rather than to the syntactic structure (embedding or parenthetical) or to the presence of the contrastive marker ‘maar’ (‘but’ in English) itself. The contrastive marker was included in the experimental items (see Table 1) to mirror examples in the literature on reportative evidentiality and commitment: even authors who claim that reportative evidentials remove all commitment still consider a contrastive marker necessary in these cases for a coherent discourse (see discussion in, e.g., AnderBois, 2014). For that reason, the fillers consisted of 16 embedding and 16 parenthetical ‘I heard’ constructions (Table 2), balanced such that, within each syntactic construction, half contained the contrastive marker and half did not. We expected minimal activity in the fillers since no commitments were violated.

As fEMG recording readily detects emotional reactions to items, the content of all items was designed under limitations. In particular, strongly valenced content is known to trigger corrugator activation, independently of the evaluation of the initial move which we hoped to elicit in this experiment (’t Hart et al., 2018). To avoid such effects, all items used non-emotive language as far as possible, and did not describe situations which we would take to be social norm violations, outside of the communicative norm violation that we are interested in (i.e., that of acting against one’s earlier commitments).

The experiment took place in the Center for Language Studies laboratory at Radboud University. The fEMG signal was recorded using Biopac hardware (MP150 module and EMG100C Electromyogram Amplifier) and Biopac’s Acqknowledge software (BIOPAC Systems, 2024). Three surface electrodes were attached to the participant; one acting as the ground (a location on the hairline with minimal palpable muscle activity), and two electrodes at bipolar corrugator recording sites (above the eyebrow in line with the pupil and on the inner side of the eyebrow). The electrode placement was based on conventions taken from the Facial Action Coding System (Ekman et al., 1972) and the guidelines for EMG developed by Fridlund and Cacioppo (1986). The electrodes were automatically referenced within the Acqknowledge software system. The electrode sites were gently cleaned with abrasive gel and alcohol to lower inter-electrode impedance. This electrical impedance (a measure of the opposition to electrical flow, in kΩ) was measured per participant prior to recording; when impedance is too high this can result in a noisy signal and the loss of meaningful fEMG signal. The fEMG signal was continuously recorded, in muscle unit action potentials (μV).

The trials were presented to the participants using OpenSesame software (Mathôt et al., 2012). Two preparatory trials familiarized the participant with the procedure. Then each participant read 96 pseudo-randomized vignettes (64 experimental and control items (16 per condition) and 32 fillers), presented line-by-line in time-locked segments. As previously mentioned, each trial was preceded by a 3,000 ms distractor image (showing a sunlit path through a forest). This segment was used to calculate baseline corrugator activity to benchmark corrugator activity during the stories. An image was used instead of, e.g., a fixation cross because the former is thought to elicit a more relaxed level of baseline corrugator activity (Fridlund & Cacioppo, 1986; ’t Hart et al., 2018).

Data files were imported into Matlab for preprocessing (The MathWorks Inc., 2026). We followed recommended preprocessing steps as laid out by van Boxtel (2010) and which were used by our lab in the earlier proof-of-method experiment (Yates et al., 2025).

The raw fEMG signal was first filtered with a 20–500 Hz band-pass filter and a 50 Hz notch filter to eliminate possible mains power electrical interference from the recorded signal. The signal was rectified and the key segments (i.e., the 3,000 ms distractor segment and 4,000 ms critical follow-up segment) were isolated. The 3,000 ms distractor segment was smoothed using the LOESS method and the mean absolute value was calculated per-trial, in order to obtain an artifact-free baseline measure of corrugator activity. The 4,000 ms follow-up segments were divided into 40 100ms bins, an interval which provides optimal temporal resolution to track rapid dynamic facial muscle activity while largely avoiding random error (van Boxtel, 2010; van Boxtel & van der Graaff, 2024). The amplitude in the follow-up segment was expressed as a percentage of the baseline mean absolute value for that trial. This method accounts for both intra- and inter-participant variation in fEMG amplitude (van Boxtel & van der Graaff, 2024). These data were then exported from MATLAB to R for statistical analysis (R Core Team, 2025).

We first tested Hypothesis (iii), which predicts lower corrugator activation in the plain assertion–congruent control condition than in the experimental conditions. Corrugator activation in the critical segment was indeed higher in the experimental conditions than in the plain assertion–congruent control condition. To determine if these differences were statistically significant, we fit a linear mixed-effects regression model predicting per-trial mean corrugator activation in the critical segment (expressed as a percentage of baseline), including fixed effects of condition and trial number, as well as random intercepts for participants and items. Statistical analyses were carried out using the ‘lme4’ package (Bates et al., 2015). Corresponding p-values were estimated using the Satterthwaite procedure as implemented in the ‘lmerTest’ package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017). The plain assertion–congruent condition served as reference level.

To better understand the difference between plain incongruent assertions and the two evidential conditions, we investigated their temporal dynamics using cluster-based permutation analyses. This method is designed for situations in which condition differences are assessed across many adjacent time points. Rather than evaluating each time bin separately, it identifies clusters of consecutive bins which exhibit a consistent effect, and assesses their significance using a permutation-based null distribution. This approach controls the family-wise error rate while remaining sensitive to temporally extended effects (Maris & Oostenveld, 2007).

In order to understand the implications of the results, it is important to revisit the rationale for using fEMG in this study. As Bartholow et al. (2001) have shown, the observation of norm violations elicits corrugator activity. In the context of this study, the relevant norm is that a speaker should not act in conflict with their prior discourse commitments. Thus, the working hypothesis of this study is that greater corrugator activation reflects a stronger perceived violation of speaker commitment.

Similarly, the plain assertion–congruent control condition (as well as the filler conditions) elicited minimal corrugator activation during the critical follow-up segment, as expected given that the speaker does not violate any prior discourse commitments. In contrast, the plain assertion–incongruent condition, which involves an explicit commitment violation, elicited significantly elevated corrugator activity relative to the control condition. These findings align with the results of the prior proof-of-method study (Yates et al., 2025), and provide further support for the reliability of our measurement approach.

The ‘I heard’ conditions also elicited significantly greater corrugator activation than the control condition, though not to the same extent as the plain assertion–incongruent condition. When a speaker used ‘I heard’ to indicate hearsay evidence for a proposition and subsequently contradicted that proposition, corrugator activity was significantly lower than when a plain assertion was contradicted. On the working hypothesis that greater corrugator activation reflects a stronger perceived commitment violation, these results suggest that plain assertions carry greater commitment to the expressed proposition than reportative statements marked with ‘I heard’, contra option (b) in the introduction. At the same time, the reportative conditions still elicited elevated corrugator activity relative to the congruent control condition, suggesting that contradictions of reportative statements are not perceived as entirely commitment-free. That makes option (a) less plausible as well. According to that option, the content introduced with Dutch ‘ik hoorde’ is just presented (that is, just put on the table for discussion by the speaker without any commitment whatsoever), as, for example, Faller (2002) proposes for the Cuzco Quechua reportative evidential –si.3 Instead, our results support option (c): the reportative evidential reduces, but does not altogether remove, the speaker’s commitment.

One way of developing this idea is provided by the account of speech reports and commitment proposed by Bary and Maier (2021). On this view, a reportative sentence introduces the reported content under the scope of an epistemic necessity operator whose modal base is determined by context. A hearer may initially adopt a relatively strong interpretation, roughly corresponding to “for all the speaker knows”. If such a statement is immediately followed by a denial of the reported content, this may initially generate a substantial expectation violation and hence a strong corrugator response. However, unlike a plain assertion, a reportative statement also permits weaker interpretations in which the relevant modal base is restricted to information obtained through hearsay. Once the hearer recognizes that such an interpretation is available, the apparent conflict may be partially resolved.

These findings suggest a discourse framework that models not only the contents of what is said but also the degree of commitment to these contents. Inspiration for such a model can be found in Northrup’s (2014) proposal where an update of a speaker’s discourse commitments consists of a pair of the propositional content and the evidential base.

A general limitation of the study is its linguistic scope. The experiment studied Dutch ‘ik hoorde’, which means that, in a strict sense, the conclusions apply to this construction in this language. Other reportative expressions in Dutch or other languages may well behave differently. Even a seemingly small change, such as from past tense ‘ik hoorde’ to present tense ‘ik hoor’, may well lead to different results. This limitation also entails that our study cannot be interpreted as falsifying claims in the literature about other reportative constructions or other languages. Although our findings at first sight seem to go against Hunter (2016), who claims that in the parenthetical construction the degree of commitment is the same as in the plain assertion, or against Murray (2014) who claims that in the embedding construction there is no commitment, their claims are about English ‘she said’ and ‘I heard’, respectively.

In addition, our study investigates how people perceive certain speech acts. This is the result of a combination of factors, of which the semantics of the reportative construction, which Murray focuses on, is only one element. More research is needed to investigate factors such as tense, Question-Under-Discussion, the perceived reliability of the information source (Koev, 2021), and the grammatical realization of the reportative expression (verb, clitic, modal). This study developed a method that can be applied in these future studies.

A second limitation is its demographic scope. It should be noted that, due to the University-centralized recruitment method, the participant sample consisted predominantly of individuals with university-level education, primarily of Dutch nationality, resulting in a relatively homogeneous WEIRD (i.e., Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) population (Henrich et al., 2010). This may raise questions about the generalization of the observed effects to populations with different sociocultural backgrounds, communicative practices, or patterns of emotional expression. Future research should investigate whether similar patterns persist in different populations.

We must also be aware of what this study should not be taken as. The results fit a gradable picture on commitment, and are certainly suggestive. Still, it would not be justified to take this experiment as proving a gradable notion of commitment in the strictest sense of the word. The alternative, a black-or-white view on commitment, is often presupposed in more formal and more philosophical work (e.g., Geurts, 2019; Singh, 2000). Although the results fit a gradable view very well, it is not excluded that they are in principle also compatible with a view where commitments themselves are categorial but what evidential markers modulate are the objects of commitments. A ‘reduced commitment’ could then mean a (full) commitment to ‘possibly p’. More research is needed on this.

Given the contributions made in this study, we maintain that fEMG is a valuable tool in exploring commitment negotiation in communication. Importantly, its sensitivity to subtle, graded affective responses suggests that fEMG can capture not only clear-cut contrasts as explored in previous work, but also the nuanced distinctions that are crucial for understanding real-time communication. Moving beyond reportative evidentiality, fEMG can be applied to more questions regarding commitments in communication. We could for example use the methodology to compare the perceived commitment attributed to speakers who assert, implicate or presuppose certain content (Mazzarella et al., 2018). Further options are to investigate the contribution of gestures or intonation, or the commitments of other conversational participants, such as the addressee. Moving beyond commitments to the truth of a proposition, we next aim to investigate ‘commitments de lingua,’ that is, a speaker’s commitment to the appropriateness of their specific word choice. In such experiments, it will be a great asset to time-lock stimuli on a word-by-word basis rather than across entire phrases, thus advancing our understanding of how communicative commitments are managed in natural discourse.

These findings also underscore the suitability of fEMG as a method for capturing such nuanced pragmatic distinctions, beyond generally agreed-upon cases. We advocate for the use of fEMG as an experimental method in pragmatics and philosophy of language, as others have advocated for the methodology’s value in language comprehension (van Berkum et al., 2023), social psychology (Bartholow et al., 2001), and political science (Schumacher et al., 2024). Our study has shown that fEMG is a promising method to progress our understanding of commitment attribution, negotiation, and avoidance in conversation, which constitute the foundation of our social lives.
See, for example, Jackendoff (1972) for ‘I think’, ‘we understand’, ‘I fear’, Asher (2000) for ‘she assured us’, Hunter (2016) for ‘she said.’
